555.description: The NPSLE outline assesses the subject's neuropsychiatric manifestations that may be attributed to SLE or other causes.

1.6.field_title: Has the subject experienced a new neurologic and/or psychiatric event since their last visit?
1.6.field_description: A “New event” is defined as a neurologic or psychiatric event that you report as active at their first Lupus Nexus visit or an event that has occurred since the last Lupus Nexus visit. If a patient has a history of neurologic or psychiatric events attributed to SLE in the past and one or more recurs, they will be recorded as new events when they recur.

1.7.field_title: A. TYPE OF EVENT, REGARDLESS OF ATTRIBUTION:

1.10.field_title: i. Acute confusional state: disturbance of consciousness or level of arousal characterized by reduced ability to focus, maintain, or shift attention, and accompanied by disturbances of cognition, mood, affect, and/or behavior. The disturbances typically develop over hours to days, tend to fluctuate during the course of the day, include hypo- and hyper-aroused states and encompass the spectrum from delirium to coma. Alternative expressions for “acute confusional state” include “encephalopathy” and “delirium” and “organic brain syndrome”.

1.32.field_title: ii. Psychosis: severe disturbance in the perception of reality characterized by delusions and/or hallucinations.

1.53.field_title: iii. Cognitive dysfunction: significant deficits in any or all of the following cognitive functions: simple or complex attention, reasoning/problem solving, executive skills (e.g., planning, organizing, sequencing), memory (e.g., learning, recall), visual-spatial processing, language (e.g., verbal fluency), and psychomotor speed. Cognitive dysfunction implies a decline from a higher level of functioning and ranges from mild impairment to severe dementia. It may or may not impede social, educational, or occupational functioning, depending on the function(s) impaired and the severity of impairment. Subjective complaints of cognitive dysfunction are common and may not be objectively verifiable. The diagnosis generally requires neuropsychological testing, ideally interpreted with the help of a neuropsychologist.

1.272.field_title: vi. Demyelinating syndrome: acute or relapsing demyelinating encephalomyelitis with evidence of discrete neurologic lesions distributed in place and time. Note that optic neuropathy, transverse myelopathy and cranial nerve palsies are also listed as separate case definitions as they can occur as isolated entities. Patients who meet criteria for these and for demyelinating syndrome that are both attributed to SLE should be classified as having both.
